content: I am trying to understand the organization of bilinearity and orthogonality in mathlib. My impression is that it is quite chaotic (and I am only looking at the linear algebra files). So please let me know whether it really is, or this is indeed just my impression.

Bilinear maps

There is a definition BilinMap for M →ₗ[R] M →ₗ[R] N in LinearAlgebra/BilinearMap.lean. Why does this exist, and why in this form?

  • Many files use the bare →ₗ[R] notation. For example, LinearAlgebra/SesquilinearForm and all duality theory of cones . In fact, even BilinearMap.lean only starts using this definition halfway through. In all these cases the reason is probably that the definition of BilinMap is not general enough, which brings me to the next point ...
  • Shouldn't BilinMap mean something more general: M →ₗ[R] N →ₗ[R] P, perhaps even sesquilinear?
  • There is also BilinForm for M →ₗ[R] M →ₗ[R] R, and I am not convinced this is useful either.

Orthogonality

  • Why is there both orthogonalBilin and orthogonal, when their difference is just the shape of the bilinear form. It duplicates a lot API.
  • Why is there dualAnnihilator/dualCoannihilator which are yet just other synonyms for orthogonalBilin with special choices for the bilinear map.
  • What is the use of B.IsOrtho x y as a def for the even shorter (!) B x y = 0? Confusingly, we also have IsOrthogonal in the same namespace which means something quite different!

If it would be up to me, I would

  • remove BilinMap and BilinForm and use the bare linear map notation throughout. Or, if we really want BilinMap (I agree that it is easier to write), define it as M →ₗ[R] N →ₗ[R] P and use it throughout.
  • remove IsOrtho and use B x y = 0. Probably rename IsOrthogonal to something that better reflects the meaning.
  • generalize orthogonalBilin to take Set M instead of Submodule R M, and to take a general bilinear map M →ₗ[R] N →ₗ[R] P (currently it assumes M = N for no reason) . Probably go further and generalize to sesquilinear maps.
  • remove orthogonal in favor of orthogonalBilin (and rename the latter to something short that we can write often without pain, say, ortho).

Please let me know why these are bad ideas, so I can understand why things are as they are.

The background is that I need to merge the functionality of #34007 into orthogonality, but I am deeply confused by the current setup. See also #mathlib4 > Unifying `Submodule.dual` and `Submodule.orthogonalBilin`

I haven't worked with this part of the library, but everything you're saying seems very reasonable. I think a lot of these names/notation come from trying to match pen and paper maths, and we can do without.
The one thing I disagree on is renaming orthogonal to ortho, it makes the meaning less transparent and more ambiguous (orthogonal? orthonormal? something else?)

Thanks. I see your point. I was just hoping for a short name because there will be several lemmas such as

lemma orthogonal_orthogonal_flip_orthogonal_eq_orthogonal (s : Set M) :
    orthogonal B (orthogonal B.flip (orthogonal B s)) = orthogonal B s

I felt ortho justified by the existing IsOrtho, but you are likely not in favor of that name either.
yeah. I agree that has to go too.

I am second-guessing myself regarding removal of BilinMap. It could be nice to have dot notation available for linear forms of this specific form. Cramming all lemmas in LinearMap with more complicated names seems less useful.

• #37381 First cleanup PR

Now primarily about removing IsOrtho.
I just realized Submodule.orthogonal is already taken by inner product space. This is quite unfortunate.

• #37389 Smaller extract from the above PR (merged)

Focuses on generalizing orthogonalBilin and redefining BilinForm.orthogonal in terms of the former.

Martin Winter said:

I just realized Submodule.orthogonal is already taken by inner product space. This is quite unfortunate.

This reinforces my believe that we will need a different name from orthogonal for the concept when the "orthogonal" does not live in the same space. Personally I have seen "orthogonal" only ever used for two subspaces of the same space (and Wikipedia seems to agree). Other potential names are "annihilator" (I have seen this only with the standard pairing with the dual space), or "dual".
I like "dual". I guess the way to think about it is that the dual space, but with an arbitrary pairing given by your bilinear product.
Do we need docs#Submodule.orthogonal ? Why not just use the same Submodule.dual definition but with the inner product plugged in?

Violeta Hernández said:

Do we need docs#Submodule.orthogonal ? Why not just use the same Submodule.dual definition but with the inner product plugged in?

My though as well. I have not worked with it, so I don't dare to make a call. Was hoping someone could explain why it exists in this form.
I can see why in certain contexts it could be nicer to have the bilinear form fixed as part of the context as opposed to having to state it in every application of orthogonal etc.

Perhaps this could be an abbrev then?
I haven't worked with this either, I'm just spitballing

Martin Winter said:

I just realized Submodule.orthogonal is already taken by inner product space. This is quite unfortunate.

Maybe we can rename to InnerProductSpace.orthogonal?
Having worked with Submodule.orthogonal recently, I'd say the current namespace has advantage for enabling dot-notation with related lemmas

My current picture is the following:

  • if the "dual" lives in a different space, then we need to pass the bilinear form as a parameter because we need to distinguish between the forward and backward directions with p vs p.flip. Currently this is Submodule.orthogonalBiln, but a shorter name is welcome, and Submodule.dual could work here.
  • orthogonality should mean the "dual" lives in the same space. So whatever Submodule.orthogonal will mean, it should not take the bilinear form as an explicit parameter but should derive it from context. This can be an abbrev of dual. If a specialized version based on inner products is needed, then it should not claim the general name Submodule.orthogonal, but maybe InnerProductSpace.orthogonal?
  • If we want to study orthogonality itself and do not want to fix the bilinear form globally, then this could be a separate BilinForm.orthogonal, which already exists, but I am not sure this is useful.
(deleted)

Weiyi Wang said:

Having worked with Submodule.orthogonal recently, I'd say the current namespace has advantage for enabling dot-notation with related lemmas

I agree we should have some version of Submodule.orthogonal for precisely this reason. The question is whether inner product spaces should claim this very general name.

For example, could inner product spaces still work with a Submodule.orthogonal like this:

def orthogonal : Submodule 𝕜 E where
  carrier := { v | ∀ u ∈ K, B u v = 0 }
  ...

where B is somehow globally set to inner 𝕜 x y?
One problem though: inner ℝ x y is a bilinear map, but inner ℂ x y is not
It is still ℝ-bilinear, does this help?
I am thinking how to get both concept under one definition
Following this idea, one way to do this is to replace Submodule.orthogonal definition, and keep the notation Kᗮ which specialize B to the inner product
If you make inner ℂ x y only ℝ-bilinear, can Submodule.orthogonal still be a ℂ-submodule?

Weiyi Wang said:

If you make inner ℂ x y only ℝ-bilinear, can Submodule.orthogonal still be a ℂ-submodule?

Hm, seems tricky

Oh wait, already the current definition of Submodule.orthogonalBilin is quite general:

def orthogonalBilin (N : Submodule R₁ M₁) (B : M₁ →ₛₗ[I₁] M₁ →ₛₗ[I₂] M) : Submodule R₁ M₁

B is not bilinear, but bi-sesquilinear, allowing different I₁ and I₂ for the first and second argument. This should be able to model inner ℂ x y, no?
Yep, that looks good
I wonder if there is already an ongoing refactor? This setup looks like it wants to have orthogonal to be redefined on top of it at some point
If you find something I would be eager to know. I am pushing for this since my PR #34007 in January. I would have expected interested parties to already comment on the PRs or this thread.
I am afraid I have not observed progress regarding my remark https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/pull/34007#discussion_r2750200326

Joël Riou said:

I am afraid I have not observed progress regarding my remark https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/pull/34007#discussion_r2750200326

Indeed, there has been no progress because I was (and am) deeply confused by the current setup of orthogonality. I cannot easily merge the proposed functionality with orthogonalBilin.

A major obstacle is that the proposed dual takes sets as opposed to submodules as input. Do we want this in general? Or should we distinguish between dual (taking submoduels) and dualSpan (taking sets) or something like this?

My suggestion was to replace B : M₁ →ₛₗ[I₁] M₁ →ₛₗ[I₂] M by B : M₁ →ₛₗ[I₂] M₁ →ₛₗ[I₂] M in docs#Submodule.orthogonalBilin. All the other definitions should be a particular case of this. I am not using very much the bilinearity/orthogonality from mathlib, but I am not completely sure we need a Set version: my guess is that it may be sufficient to have a lemma which would characterize the orthogonal of the submodule spanned by a set.
Your suggested change is part of #37389

The rationale for the set version is that one wants to talk about submodules cut out by finitely many equalities. These are "orthogonals of FG submodules", but more naturally "duals of finite sets". See also PointedCone.DualFG

(Apparently my original response never got sent.) As someone who worked on this corner of the library since very long ago: the reason for all this mess is that we started out with everything specialized to docs#BilinForm and only incrementally generalized to maps when someone needed it. Nobody took the time to turn it into a coherent whole until now, so thank you very much for that!
And it is important to note that BilinForm used to be a structure with additive in each component and homogeneous in each component. And there used to be a second structure for sesquilinear..

Thanks for the information, this helps understanding what is going on. I better dont promise too much cleanup since I primarily need to get polyhedral math going. I have some students who maybe can work on it though. We will see. But it is good to talk about how a cleanup should look like.

Has anyone a tendency towards one of these options:

  1. we remove BilinMap and BilinForm and work with the bare expressions M →ₗ[R] N →ₗ[R] P (or better, their sesquilinear versions) throughout?
  2. we keep BilinMap and BilinForm, and (try to) never use the bare form. This allows us to use dot notation for bilinearity lemmas. Also, moving bilinearity lemmas into BilinMap/BilinForm namespaces does unclutter the LinearMap namespace.
  3. we use the bare form throughout, but still have namespaces BilinMap/BilinForm for uncluttering LinearMap; disadvantage is that we can't use dot notation.

I think option 2 is the best: since BilinMap/BilinForm are abbrevs there is no real technical drawback between this and the bare LinearMap spelling, and we gain dot notation and uncluttering of namespaces.

Joël Riou said:

I am not using very much the bilinearity/orthogonality from mathlib, but I am not completely sure we need a Set version: my guess is that it may be sufficient to have a lemma which would characterize the orthogonal of the submodule spanned by a set.

I think I agree now. I just reworked #34007 to be maximally general, and I also replaced Set by Submodule. This required me to duplicate some lemmas to have set-versions (like e.g. mem_span), but some other lemmas could be deleted (like dual_span), so I call it equal. The real reason I think dual (or orthogonal or whatever) should be on Submodule, not Set, is that this clearly separates the functionality of span from dual. I think, whatever the reason is, it should apply to PointedCone.dual as well. So I currently think the latter should be rewritten away from the current set-version. I will try this eventually.

Martin Winter said:

I think, whatever the reason is, it should apply to PointedCone.dual as well. So I currently think the latter should be rewritten away from the current set-version. I will try this eventually.

I tested this change for cone duality in #37951, and I think I like it better than what we currently have.

Another PR: #37963 moves orthogonalBilin to its own file and adds the functionality of #34007. I hope the naming problem becomes evident with lemmas such as orthogonalBilin_flip_orthogonalBilin_orthogonalBilin_flip.

Weiyi Wang said:

Following this idea, one way to do this is to replace Submodule.orthogonal definition, and keep the notation Kᗮ which specialize B to the inner product

After #37389, the current definition of Submodule.orthogonal for inner product spaces can be replaced (and eventually dropped) with relatively few fixes necessary:

def orthogonal : Submodule 𝕜 E := orthogonalBilin (innerₛₗ 𝕜) K

But what seems not to work is

notation:1200 K "ᗮ" => orthogonalBilin (innerₛₗ 𝕜) K

because 𝕜 is unknown in this notation.

But I just realize I can do

notation:1200 K "ᗮ" => orthogonalBilin (innerₛₗ _) K

Now, this new definition for orthogonal requires to insert rw [innerₛₗ_apply_apply] over and over at many places because inner product spaces use inner as a plain function, not the bilinear map innerₛₗ. I find this weird... and I cannot foresee whether this will cause problems later.
